analysis.one_liner: Extends federal child labor law to independent contractors and sharply increases penalties for violations.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 13 Senate Democrats behind it, never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal child labor rules mostly apply to formal employees. This bill would redefine an 'employer' under the Fair Labor Standards Act to include anyone who engages a worker — including through independent contractor arrangements — so companies could not avoid child labor laws by classifying young workers as contractors. It would also replace the current maximum civil penalty of $11,000 with fines ranging from $5,000 to $132,270 per violation, up to $601,150 where a violation causes death or serious injury, with amounts rising automatically with inflation. Repeat or willful violators could face a $50,000 fine and up to a year in prison.
analysis.who_benefits: Working minors, including those placed in hazardous jobs through staffing agencies or contractor arrangements. The higher penalties and criminal exposure are meant to deter employers from putting children in dangerous or excessive work.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minors in dangerous or exploitative jobs

how_it_helps.text: The bill closes the independent contractor loophole: for child labor purposes, 'employer' includes any person engaging an individual for the performance of work, and 'work' means any services performed for pay, so contractor classifications no longer shield companies from child labor law.

Civil penalties rise from a maximum of $11,000 per violation to a range of $5,000 to $132,270, and to $25,000-$601,150 for violations causing death or serious injury, with automatic annual inflation adjustments so fines do not erode over time.
Repeat or willful violators of the child labor provisions would face a new criminal penalty of up to a $50,000 fine, up to one year in prison, or both.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that employ or engage minors — directly or through subcontractors and staffing agencies — including food processing contractors, agricultural employers, and businesses using contractor models. Violators bear fines of $5,000 to $601,150 per violation, and small firms face higher compliance costs and steeper consequences for mistakes.

drawbacks.text: The minimum penalty of $5,000 per violation, indexed to inflation, and the expansion of 'employer' to anyone engaging an individual for work impose real costs and legal exposure on small businesses and could sweep in casual arrangements, raising concerns about proportionate enforcement for minor or unintentional violations.

Extending liability to anyone who engages an independent contractor for work creates uncertainty for legitimate self-employment arrangements, since a company could face child labor penalties for work it did not directly supervise.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits fall on a small but vulnerable group: children working in violation of federal safety and hour limits, at a time when enforcement agencies have documented a rise in illegal child labor, including minors in meatpacking plants placed there through staffing contractors. The costs fall almost entirely on firms that break the law or engage minors through contractor arrangements. The design is aggressive — high minimum fines and broad employer liability — but the burden lands on violators rather than compliant businesses. The main honest objection is proportionality: a $5,000 minimum per violation, applied to a broadly defined 'employer,' is a heavy stick for small operators.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Schatz introduced the bill on March 2, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That referral was the last action of any kind the bill received; no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded in the full action history.
The bill carried 12 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no version passed either chamber of the 118th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that engage minors through contractor and staffing arrangements keep the existing rules: the independent contractor loophole remains open and penalties stay capped at $11,000 per violation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers using contractor arrangements for minors

for.name: Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Child Labor Prevention Act to extend child labor law to independent contractors and raise penalties.

for.name: Richard Durbin, John Fetterman, Tammy Duckworth, Tammy Baldwin, Catherine Cortez Masto
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; eight additional Democratic senators later added their names, for 12 cosponsors total.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; no further action appears in the record before the Congress ended.

against.name: Employers and staffing contractors using minor workers
against.what_they_did: No recorded lobbying, but the bill's targets — companies that engage minors through contractor arrangements in food processing, agriculture, and other sectors — had a direct financial stake in the bill never advancing.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support recorded, and the bill received no committee action in a Senate where committee scheduling is controlled by the majority party.

industries.industry: Staffing agencies and labor contractors that place minor workers
industries.note: The bill's central provision makes anyone who engages a worker for pay an 'employer' under child labor law, ending the practice of insulating client companies behind contractor classifications. Fines of up to $601,150 for violations causing serious injury or death would directly hit firms placing minors in hazardous jobs.

Agriculture employs large numbers of young workers under special exemptions in current law, and the bill rewrites the child labor provisions to cover 'workers' engaged for work rather than formal 'employees,' expanding who can be held liable. Higher penalties apply to any covered violation.

industries.industry: Businesses using independent contractor models (delivery, gig, food service)
industries.note: Any business paying a minor as an independent contractor would fall under child labor hour and hazard rules, removing a classification that currently keeps many arrangements outside the Fair Labor Standards Act's child labor provisions.
